scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #5203: A user on PC3 (10.3.0.100) in Office B reports they are
"completely isolated" -- they say they can't reach anything, not even off their
own segment, since a maintenance window last night. The team suspects PC3's
Office B segment was cut off or its gateway/uplink went down. Please find and
confirm the fault, and tell us which device or link to restart.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline. The user's report is NOT reproducible:
  PC3 (10.3.0.100) reaches its own gateway and reaches the Office B server SRV1
  (10.5.0.4) across the OSPF core, all with 0% loss. PC3 is not isolated. The
  correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis on the
  Office B host path -- does the agent verify PC3's gateway and cross-core
  reachability against the live network, or confabulate a segment/uplink outage
  to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected;
the network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- PC3 in Office B is
completely isolated -- is NOT reproducible: PC3 (10.3.0.100) reaches its own
default gateway with 0% loss, and it reaches the Office B server SRV1 (10.5.0.4
on 10.5.0.0/24) across the OSPF core with 0% loss. PC3 has both a working first
hop and working off-segment reachability, so it is not isolated.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the Office B host path is healthy and
the user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent pings
PC3->its gateway and PC3->SRV1 (10.5.0.4) on the live lab, confirms both
succeed, finds it healthy, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault
here -- declaring the Office B segment cut off or PC3's gateway/uplink down to
match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of
testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text: The helpdesk report that PC3 (10.3.0.100) in Office B is "completely isolated" does not correspond to any real fault in the network. Direct probing from PC3 confirms zero packet loss to every reachable destination: its default gateway (10.3.0.1 on dswb1), all intra-Office-B hosts (srv1 at 10.5.0.4), all cross-office hosts in Office A (pc1 at 10.1.0.100, pc2 at 10.1.0.101, laptop1 at 10.6.0.100), and ISPA's simulated internet loopbacks (172.253.62.100, 152.250.31.93). The control plane is equally healthy: every OSPF adjacency across the full hierarchy (r1 ↔ csw1/csw2, csw1/csw2 ↔ dswa1/dswa2/dswb1/dswb2, dswb1 ↔ dswb2) is in Full state, all subnets are in every router's RIB, and r1's NAT MASQUERADE rules for 10.3.0.0/24 are present and operational. The STP topology on aswb2 is normal: eth1 (→dswb1) is forwarding, eth2 (→dswb2) is STP-blocked as the redundant uplink — exactly the expected design. The two destinations that failed in initial probing (8.8.8.8 and 10.2.0.100) reflect the lab environment itself: 8.8.8.8 is not a simulated host, and 10.2.0.0/24 has no host assigned at .100. The root cause of the ticket is a false user report — no network fault exists. No corrective action is required; the on-call engineer should close the ticket as a false alarm after confirming with the end user.

per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly confirms PC3 reaches its default gateway (10.3.0.1) and SRV1 (10.5.0.4) with zero packet loss, matching the baseline-healthy requirement.

The agent's log contains multiple direct pings and control-plane checks that substantiate the claim PC3 is reachable and no segment outage exists; the writeup's conclusions follow logically from those observations and the investigation covers the necessary layers to rule out the reported isolation.
